title: Graph World Models for Verified and Efficient Long-Horizon LLM Task Planning
content:
GAVEL: Graph World Models for Verified and Efficient Long-Horizon LLM Task Planning
Ruiyang Wang and colleagues present GAVEL, which verifies and repairs long-horizon LLM robot plans against an explicit graph world model holding object relations, action preconditions and effects, and probabilistic beliefs over unobserved locations.

Abstract
Large language models (LLMs) provide a flexible interface for long-horizon robot planning, but generated plans often fail to respect embodiment constraints, recover from planning errors, or reason effectively under partial observability. We present GAVEL, a framework for verifying and repairing long-horizon LLM planning built around an explicit graph world model. The graph represents relevant object-relations, action pre-conditions and effects, and probabilistic beliefs over unobserved object locations. This model can predict the consequences of LLM-generated actions before execution, detect violations, and repair those whose corrections follow directly from the world model. This method also reserves LLM replanning solely for errors requiring semantic reasoning. For multi-task instructions, GAVEL reasons over distributions of possible object locations to reorder remaining subtasks and minimize expected search cost. We evaluate GAVEL on BEHAVIOR-1K across 100 single long-horizon tasks and 500 multi-task instructions. With Qwen3-8B, GAVEL improves single-task success from 41.2% to 91.8% and multi-task success from 19.9% to 92.6%. Distributional belief reasoning also reduces travel distance by approximately 5.4% compared with a static variant. These improvements show that an explicit graph world model harness can substantially improve the reliability and efficiency of long-horizon embodied planning across compact and frontier hosted LLM capabilities.

report.summary: GAVEL adds an explicit graph world model outside the LLM to verify and repair long-horizon robot plans, lifting BEHAVIOR-1K task success from 41.2% to 91.8%.
report.background: LLMs are increasingly used as the reasoning layer for long-horizon embodied agents, converting natural-language goals into sequences of actions. But LLM planners are prone to hallucinating actions that violate physical or embodiment constraints, failing to recover once a step fails, and ignoring partial observability, where objects may be in unknown locations. Classical task planners solve these issues with explicit symbolic models, yet they struggle with open-ended language goals and cannot be authored by hand for every environment. GAVEL takes a hybrid route: it keeps the LLM as the flexible plan generator but pairs it with an explicit graph world model that encodes object relations, action preconditions and effects, and probabilistic beliefs over unobserved object locations. This mirrors a broader industry shift toward neuro-symbolic architectures and external verification harnesses that constrain LLM output rather than relying on model scale alone.
key_points: The graph world model simulates actions before they are executed, predicting their consequences. When a predicted violation follows directly from the model, GAVEL repairs the plan locally instead of calling the LLM again, reserving expensive semantic replanning only for errors that genuinely need language reasoning.

Belief reasoning over unknown object locations pays off: GAVEL tracks probability distributions over where unobserved objects might be and reorders remaining subtasks to minimize expected search cost, cutting travel distance by about 5.4% versus a static version.

Results on BEHAVIOR-1K with Qwen3-8B are striking: single long-horizon task success climbs from 41.2% to 91.8% across 100 tasks, and multi-task instruction success rises from 19.9% to 92.6% across 500 instructions.

Most of the gain comes from the verification harness, not the model. A compact open-weight model paired with the graph world model outperforms bare planning by a wide margin, suggesting reliability is an architecture problem as much as a capability problem.
report.impact: For the AI industry, GAVEL is evidence that the bottleneck in agentic systems is verification, not raw model intelligence. Teams chasing better long-horizon agents may get more return from an external world model and consistency checker than from a larger LLM. For developers, it validates a practical pattern: let the model propose, let a symbolic layer dispose, and keep repair cheap by handling structural errors without another inference call, which also reduces latency and token cost. For regular users, the near-term effect is more dependable household and warehouse robots that fail less often mid-task and waste less time searching for misplaced objects. The caveat: the harness must be built per domain, so generalization beyond the modeled environment remains the open question.
report.tools: To follow up, look at BEHAVIOR-1K and the OmniGibson simulator for long-horizon embodied benchmarks. For symbolic planning and validation, PDDLStream, Fast Downward, and the VAL plan validator are the standard companions. Scene-graph libraries such as Open3D or 3D Scene Graph tooling help build the relational layer, and open-weight planners like Qwen3-8B are the natural testbed for reproducing the harness-versus-model ablation.
